blocks.text: First Chronicles 9 presents genealogical registers of those who inhabited their possessions after the exile to Babylon. The chapter records residents of Jerusalem and surrounding settlements, organized by tribal affiliation and family houses. It documents priests and Levites who returned to service, connecting the post-exilic community to the preexilic structures that had characterized the earlier kingdom.

The chapter establishes its historical frame clearly: after Judah's captivity to Babylon due to transgression, the first inhabitants who dwelt in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the Nethinim. These genealogies thus document the reconstitution of the community and its leadership structures following the exile.

Among Jerusalem's inhabitants were representatives from multiple tribal traditions: Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Prominent individuals such as Uthai (of Judah, through Perez), Sallu (of Benjamin, through Meshullam), and others are listed as heads of their fathers' houses, each with genealogical credentials and household counts. These entries document the organizational structure through which the restored community reestablished itself in the city.

The chapter documents priestly genealogies, including Azariah, identified as ruler of the house of God and traced through Zadok and Ahitub, as well as families such as Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Adaiah, and Maasai. These priests, numbering over 1,760 and described as very able men for the work of the service of the house of God, represent the reinstitution of priestly leadership and cultic function. Their genealogical documentation connects them to the preexilic priesthood.

The chapter records Levites who returned to service, including Shemaiah of the sons of Merari, and others such as Mattaniah (descended from the line of Asaph), Obadiah (descended from Jeduthun), and Bakbakkar. These genealogies connect the restored Levites to established preexilic lineages and musical/liturgical traditions, indicating the restoration of Levitical functions within the post-exilic temple community.
